topic: Detecting Walking-Dead States in Games with an AI Agent

key_points: Anchor source for the exact topic: 'Sierra softlock analyzer' — a static-analysis tool that decompiles Sierra SCI games, abstract-interprets the AST into a guarded room-transition graph, finds softlocks ('states where the game still accepts input but victory has quietly become impossible'), then derives, verifies, compiles and installs guards that prevent them.
Nothing is declared per title: start room, victory room, death signal and debug flags are all discovered from the game's own code.

Pipeline stages: decompile -> extract -> lift -> analyze -> derive -> patch. Decompilation uses a fork of sci-tools (JSON-IR branch, ~277 additive lines) to keep a typed control-flow AST instead of throwing it away.
Core insight: only one-way edges BETWEEN strongly-connected components can strand you, 'which is what makes the problem finite' (101 rooms -> 27 SCCs, 40 gating registers in LSL2).

Guard placement rule: place the guard at the last point where the player can still comply; demanding the player drop something they can no longer drop is a wall, which the project treats as worse than the bug.
Guards carry negative literals too: the LSL2 Spinach Dip is fatal to be HOLDING in rm138, so the fix refuses the crossing while you still have it.

Safety property enforced in the pipeline: 're-verified the guarded model to prove the guards introduce no new softlocks' and 'the pipeline refuses to emit anything if the guards fail verification, or if a script it edited will not compile.'
Deliberately keeps avoidable deaths in: it distinguishes unwinnable states from avoidable deaths by reachability, not by death conditions — deaths that hint at what you need stay.
Patch format is Sierra's own loose script.NNN override; RESOURCE.MAP and volumes are never modified, so deleting the files reverts. Ships guard modes Full / Lite / Off.
Validated on 5 games across both engine eras (SCI0 1988 -> SCI1.1 1992) with no game-specific analysis code: LSL2, KQ4, KQ6, Laura Bow 2, KQ5.
Known limit: state explosion in Quest For Glory games — the analyzer cannot complete; authors suspect abstracting away player stats/combat/health consumables would fix it.
Honest limitation stated by the author: no game has had a single continuous start-to-finish run on a patched build yet (KQ5 comes closest, tested row by row).
'Stuck in the Middle: Generating Levels without (or with) Softlocks' (FDG 2025) — formalizes a softlock as 'the player has not won or lost, but cannot make progress toward the goal.'
Key distinction the article must make: completability (a path exists from the start) does NOT imply softlock-freedom (a path to the goal exists from EVERY reachable place).
Method: constraint-based reachability categorization of locations during level generation — classify each location as forward-reachable, backward-reachable, or a sink.

Prevention rule: every location forward-reachable from the start must also be backward-reachable from the goal, unless it is a sink (an area where the player inevitably loses, e.g. falling off the bottom).
The same categorization can intentionally generate softlocks and repair existing levels to remove them.
Cost data: generating levels without softlocks takes ~3-5x longer than plain path reachability; with softlocks 3-8x; with the extra constraint that softlocks are disconnected from sinks, 3-15x.
Prior art it cites for model-based softlock detection: Petri nets, hyperstate space graphs, computation tree logic.
'Softlock Detection for Super Metroid with Computation Tree Logic' (Mawhorter & Smith, FDG 2021) — the canonical academic reference for automated softlock detection.
Frames the problem: 'level designs can contain errors called softlocks where a player traversing the level in an unintended manner can become permanently stuck.'
Uses CTL (Computation Tree Logic) model checking over a model of the game rather than brute-force play, so detection is exhaustive over the model.

Its follow-up line of work (Mawhorter & Smith, 'Comprehensive and Instantly Responsive Player Assistance using Binary Decision Diagrams') replaces explicit search with symbolic BFS over a BDD-encoded transition relation — reachability without paying a cost linear in the number of states.

That BDD approach supports exactly the queries a walking-dead detector needs: 'can I collect item A without beating boss B?', the complete set of reachable states, and shortest-path advice from any reachable state to any goal.
Reports the honest evolution of the work: an explicit BFS-style algorithm over a symbolic abstraction was tried first and led to the BDD formulation.
TITAN — 'Leveraging LLM Agents for Automated Video Game Testing' (Zhejiang Univ. / NetEase Fuxi AI Lab / SMU). The LLM-agent counterpoint to static analysis.

Four components worth copying: (1) perceive and abstract high-dimensional game states, (2) proactively optimize and prioritize available actions, (3) long-horizon reasoning with action trace memory and reflective self-correction, (4) LLM-based oracles that detect functional/logic bugs with diagnostic reports.
Reported results: 95% task completion vs 82% for the best automated baseline, and 15 bugs detected vs 9; detects four previously unknown bugs.
Ablation: the Reflective Reasoning Module contributes the most; all components are indispensable.
Deployed in eight real-world game QA pipelines — evidence the approach is production-viable, not just a benchmark result.
Explicit motivation is the state-action space and long-complex-task reasoning limits of earlier LLM game-playing approaches.
The live-ops/viewpoint competitor: softlocks are a data problem, not just a design problem — 'players get stuck unable to progress while the game keeps running' is invisible to crash telemetry.
Core argument: the silent majority — 'most players who hit it never report it — they just leave', so 'the worse the problem, the quieter it often is' and a quiet inbox proves nothing.

Prescribed confirmation path: add stuck-state detection plus an in-game report button, capture every failure with stack trace, device, build and breadcrumbs regardless of whether the player says anything.
Then group identical failures into one ranked issue with an occurrence count, tie each to the build it happened on, and verify the signature disappears in the next release.
'It works on my machine is a trap': the dev machine is the single least representative device the game will ever run on.
The origin of the TERM: Jimmy Maher's design criticism names the 'walking-dead syndrome' — the player continues playing a game that has, unbeknownst to them, been rendered unwinnable.

Historical scope: 'Virtually all adventure games of the 1980s, including even the best designs from the textual realm of Infocom, offered plenty of opportunities to lock yourself out of victory in the course of their normal interactivity.'

Design-side observation the article can quote: designs that strain hardest to make the walking-dead syndrome impossible (the later Lucasfilm Games adventures) are often forced into contrivances that 'arguably sacrifice too much of that all-important illusion of freedom.'

Concrete worked example it gives: Uninvited — skip looking in the mailbox in the Front Yard, step inside, and the front door locks behind you forever. 'As soon as you go inside, you become a walking dead.'
Distinguishes accidental dead ends from 'intentional traps inserted' to pad length — a useful taxonomy for the intro.

stats.fact: Show HN 'Automatically detect and patch walking-dead states in Sierra games' reached 161 points, posted 2026-08-19 — the topic has fresh, verifiable public interest.
Lucasartsifier's LSL2 run: 101 rooms, 27 strongly-connected components, 40 gating registers, 15 item softlocks + 1 disjunctive group; 117/118 scripts recompiled into 10 patch files.

Lucasartsifier clean-room timings on ubuntu:24.04 against King's Quest IV: decompile 14s, scicompile build 1m54s, analysis (--report) 1m20s, full run through patch emission 1m23s -> 5 loose patch files.
The analyzer is ~7,200 lines of Python 3 using only the standard library — Tarjan, BFS and fixpoints, no numpy/networkx/solver bindings.
Wuji (NetEase) analyzed 1,349 real bugs from four commercial online games; one benchmark game had 30 dedicated testers and roughly $2M/year in direct bug losses.
Wuji found 3 previously unknown bugs in commercial games, later confirmed by the developers.
TITAN reports 95% task completion (vs 82% best baseline) and 15 bugs detected (vs 9), and is deployed in eight real-world game QA pipelines.
RLBGameTester's DQN agent reached 92.3% accuracy detecting collision bugs and 88.7% on progression-blocking issues across 15 test levels.
VideoGameQA-Bench: best-reported visual glitch-detection accuracy rose from 57.2% to 82.8% with GPT-4o; the best open-weight model (Qwen-2.5-VL) reached 70.0%.
EA SEED: testing all maps and modes of Battlefield V for one hour requires 2,304 man-hours — 288 people testing every day.
EA/DICE production deployment reality: 250 concurrent agents across 5 servers in Battlefield 2042 versus only 7 in Dead Space, and ~45 seconds of reset overhead per episode.
EA SEED agents could navigate 80% of test levels within 24 hours of training from scratch, finding bugs in areas human testers had cleared for weeks.
Generating levels without softlocks costs ~3-5x plain path reachability; with the extra sink-disconnection constraint it costs 3-15x.
A vendor case study claims an RL agent covers ~10M unique states/day against ~2,000/week for a 5-person manual QA team, and finds 50+ softlock incidents per project.

angles: Name the term properly: 'walking dead' is adventure-game design criticism (Jimmy Maher, filfre, 2015) for the player who keeps playing a game that has already become unwinnable — it is a UX/human state, whereas 'softlock' (Super Mario Wiki, FDG papers) is the mechanical state that causes it. Most coverage conflates the two; separating them is the article's first useful move.

Completability is not softlock-freedom. A level can be winnable from the start and still strand a player who took a legal detour. This single distinction is the whole problem statement, and it comes straight from the FDG 2025 reachability-categorization paper.

Static vs dynamic is a false binary — the honest framing is which one you can actually verify. Static analysis gives a proof obligation (re-verify the guarded model). RL/LLM agents give coverage and reproducible traces but no proof. Say so plainly.

Why softlocks are invisible: crash telemetry catches the crash, not the stuck player. Cite the silent-majority mechanism (most stuck players never file a report) plus the review-bias version of the same problem — the worse the bug, the quieter it is.

The one-way edge is the whole problem. Only irreversible transitions BETWEEN freely-wanderable regions can strand a player; the Lucasartsifier's SCC condensation is what makes detection finite. Explaining 'condense, then look only at the one-way edges between components' is the key algorithmic takeaway.

Guard placement is a design decision, not just a patch. Refuse at the last moment the player can still comply; never demand they undo something they can no longer undo. A guard that creates a new wall is worse than the bug it fixes.

Two-sided guards: some items are fatal to hold at a location (the LSL2 Spinach Dip), so a correct guard set includes negative literals ('refuse if the player HAS this'), not just positive ones ('refuse if the player LACKS this'). This is the detail almost no competitor article covers.

Verification is the differentiator. The pipeline refuses to emit a patch if the guards fail re-verification or a touched script will not compile — 'NEW softlocks introduced: none' is an asserted, checked property, not a hope.

Don't guard everything: keep deaths that are still avoidable from where the player stands. Those deaths teach the player what the puzzle wants. Reachability, not the death condition, decides which deaths survive.

LLM agents as testers: TITAN's four-part recipe (state abstraction, action prioritization, trace memory with reflective self-correction, LLM oracles) plus its 95%/82% and 15-vs-9 numbers, and the fact that it is deployed in eight pipelines.

The real enemy is state explosion, not the algorithm. The analyzer handles 101 rooms / 27 SCCs but simply cannot complete on Quest For Glory games. Anyhow article that promises 'just add agents' is hiding this.

Coverage-driven beats bug-specific rewards. EA SEED's finding — reward thorough exploration rather than hunting specific bugs — is the most transferable lesson for anyone building a playtesting agent, and it is why an exploration agent finds exploits nobody scripted.
Scale numbers as a gut-punch for the intro: 2,304 man-hours to test Battlefield V's maps and modes for one hour, i.e. 288 testers a day. That is the number that justifies automation.

outline: H2: What a walking-dead state actually is — and how it differs from a softlock, a crash, and a death you can still avoid
H2: Why walking-dead states stay invisible: crash telemetry, the silent majority, and why the worst bug is the quietest
H2: Completability is not softlock-freedom: the one distinction the whole problem rests on
H2: The static-analysis approach: decompile, abstract-interpret, condense into SCCs, then hunt only the one-way edges
H2: Finding the stranding: which items are required later, obtainable now, and irreversibly missable
H2: Guard placement: refuse at the last moment the player can still comply
H2: Two-sided guards: when the fatal mistake is carrying an item, not forgetting one
H2: Prove it or don't ship it: re-verifying the guarded model for NEW softlocks
H2: Know what to leave alone: distinguishing unwinnable states from informative, avoidable deaths
H2: The dynamic approach: RL and LLM agents that explore their way into dead ends
H2: Static vs dynamic vs hybrid: which one you can actually verify
